Learning what we never observe

Maximum likelihood, expectation–maximization and hidden-variable models
Yuwen Huang
Advanced Machine Learning and Deep Learning · HKUST (Guangzhou)

→ next · ← back · F full screen · H keys
Why today

In real data, the key variable is often never written down

All four use expectation–maximization (EM) or its hard-label form, k-means.

Warm-up · Retrieve before we build

Two facts from earlier lectures that EM reuses

A coin shows 7 heads in 10 flips. What is our best guess of its heads chance?
Answer. 7/10: count heads, divide by flips. Today we prove this is the maximum-likelihood answer.
Monte Carlo (Lecture 4): with 4 times as many samples, the error shrinks by a factor of …
Answer. 2: with mmm samples the typical error is σ/m\sigma/\sqrt mσ/m​. With spread σ=1\sigma=1σ=1: 1/25=0.21/\sqrt{25}=0.21/25​=0.2, 1/100=0.11/\sqrt{100}=0.11/100​=0.1; so 4 times the samples halves the error, 0.2/0.1=2=40.2/0.1=2=\sqrt40.2/0.1=2=4​.

Both return: counting in EM's maximization step, sampling for too many hidden cases.

The running example

The two-coin game: we see the flips, never the coin

We seethree records, HH, HT, TT (H = heads, T = tails); both flips of a record come from one coin.
Hiddenwhich coin made each record; a new fair toss each round, so the coins can differ.
Goalestimate the heads chances θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​ from the three records alone.

Every idea today is first worked out on these three records, by hand.

The story

Eight questions; each answer raises the next

SectionQuestion on the coinsAnswer
1 CountingIf we are told each coin, what are θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​?count heads, divide
2 Hidden variablesNot told: how likely is a record, and which coin made it?a sum; Bayes' rule
3 EMCan we still count?yes, with soft labels: split each record by its posterior
4 Why EM climbsDoes every round improve the fit?yes: each round raises a lower bound that touches the log-likelihood
5 MixturesWhat if coins become bell curves?the same EM, now clustering points
6 Hidden chainsWhat if the coin switches between flips?sum-product on a chain
7 Monte Carlo EMToo many hidden cases to add up?sample them
8 Trusting the fitIs the answer right, and the only one?restart from several guesses; check the data can pin down every unknown

Each section runs the same five steps, so you always know where you are.

Learning objectives

By the end of today you can do six things

1 · Countfit a model when nothing is hidden, and say why counting is the maximum-likelihood answer.You can answer: why is 7 heads in 10 flips fitted by 7/10?
2 · Infercompute a record's probability with a hidden variable, and the posterior of that variable.You can answer: which coin probably made HH?
3 · Run EMby hand: E-step (expectation: soft labels) and M-step (maximization: count and divide).You can answer: how do soft labels become new heads chances?
4 · Provethat no EM round lowers the log-likelihood (how well θ\thetaθ fits the data), with one inequality.You can answer: can an EM round ever make the fit worse?
5 · RecognizeEM inside clustering for vector search, tokenizers, crowd labelling and reasoning models.You can answer: where is the hidden coin in a tokenizer?
6 · Judgea fit: a start that gets stuck, the names A and B swapped, or more unknowns than the data can fix.You can answer: why may EM swap the names A and B?

Six skills, one example: three records of two coin flips.

1 · Learning by counting · A · Idea

If the friend tells us the coin, we just count

Goal: learn θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​, the heads chances of coins A and B, from the records HH, HT, TT. First the easy case: the friend also tells us which coin made each record.

Recall the gameA fair toss picks coin A or B, flipped twice. Normally we see only the flips; for now the friend also names the coin.
Estimateheads ÷ flips: θA=34\theta_A=\tfrac34θA​=43​ and θB=02=0\theta_B=\tfrac02=0θB​=20​=0.
Two questionsWhy is counting the best guess? Can coin B really never land heads?

With the coin told, learning is counting: heads ÷ flips, coin by coin.

1 · Learning by counting · C · Theorem

For any coin, the counted fraction maximizes the likelihood

Theorem 1 (maximum likelihood by counting). Independent flips of a coin with heads chance θ\thetaθ show hhh heads and ttt tails. Then ℓ(θ)=hln⁡θ+tln⁡(1−θ)\ell(\theta)=h\ln\theta+t\ln(1-\theta)ℓ(θ)=hlnθ+tln(1−θ) is largest at θ^=hh+t\cG{\hat\theta=\tfrac{h}{h+t}}θ^=h+th​.
the best heads chance is the fraction of heads seen.
ℓ′(θ)=hθ−t1−θ=0\ell'(\theta)=\dfrac h\theta-\dfrac t{1-\theta}=0ℓ′(θ)=θh​−1−θt​=0
Slope zero. Coin A: h=3, t=1h=3,\ t=1h=3, t=1.
h(1−θ)=tθ⇒θ=hh+th(1-\theta)=t\theta\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac h{h+t}h(1−θ)=tθ⇒θ=h+th​
Times θ(1−θ)\theta(1-\theta)θ(1−θ). Coin A: 33+1=34\tfrac3{3+1}=\tfrac343+13​=43​.
ℓ′′(θ)=−hθ2−t(1−θ)2<0\ell''(\theta)=-\dfrac h{\theta^2}-\dfrac t{(1-\theta)^2}\lt0ℓ′′(θ)=−θ2h​−(1−θ)2t​<0
Curves down: one top.
h=0h=0h=0: ℓ=tln⁡(1−θ)\ell=t\ln(1-\theta)ℓ=tln(1−θ), falling
Top at θ=0\theta=0θ=0. Coin B: 02=0\tfrac02=020​=0.
t=0t=0t=0: ℓ=hln⁡θ\ell=h\ln\thetaℓ=hlnθ, rising

Whatever the counts, the likelihood peaks at heads ÷ flips.

1 · Learning by counting · B · On the coins

Counting says coin B can never land heads

Coin B showed T, T. Theorem 1 gives θB=00+2=0\theta_B=\tfrac{0}{0+2}=0θB​=0+20​=0.

Too sure. Suppose B is flipped again and shows HT:

p(HT∣B)=θB(1−θB)=0⋅1=0.p(\text{HT}\mid B)=\theta_B(1-\theta_B)=0\cdot1=0.p(HT∣B)=θB​(1−θB​)=0⋅1=0.

Its log-likelihood is ln⁡0=−∞\ln0=-\inftyln0=−∞: the model calls a record we could easily see impossible.

Weak evidence: a fair coin shows TT with chance 12⋅12=14\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac1421​⋅21​=41​.

Fix: add one imagined head and one imagined tail (dashed):

θB=0+12+2=14,p(HT∣B)=14⋅34=316.\theta_B=\frac{0+1}{2+2}=\frac14,\qquad p(\text{HT}\mid B)=\frac14\cdot\frac34=\frac3{16}.θB​=2+20+1​=41​,p(HT∣B)=41​⋅43​=163​.

Two tails cannot prove heads impossible; imagined flips keep every outcome possible.

1 · Learning by counting · C · Theorem

Laplace's rule: the posterior mean adds one head and one tail

Theorem 2 (Laplace's rule). Put a uniform prior on θ\thetaθ, then see hhh heads and ttt tails. The posterior mean is E[θ∣flips]=h+1h+t+2\cG{\mathbb E[\theta\mid\text{flips}]=\tfrac{h+1}{h+t+2}}E[θ∣flips]=h+t+2h+1​.
add one imagined head and one imagined tail, then count.

Bayes (prior 1), then average θ\thetaθ.

(h+1)!h!=h+1\tfrac{(h+1)!}{h!}=h+1h!(h+1)!​=h+1, (h+t+1)!(h+t+2)!=1h+t+2\tfrac{(h+t+1)!}{(h+t+2)!}=\tfrac1{h+t+2}(h+t+2)!(h+t+1)!​=h+t+21​. ■\blacksquare■

Coin B: 0+12+2=14\tfrac{0+1}{2+2}=\tfrac142+20+1​=41​. Coin A: 3+14+2=23\tfrac{3+1}{4+2}=\tfrac234+23+1​=32​, pulled from 34\tfrac3443​ toward 12\tfrac1221​.

1 · Learning by counting · C · Theorem, rewritten

Laplace's rule pulls the count toward 1/2 by a weight ε\varepsilonε

Laplace's rule mixes the counted fraction with the even guess 12\tfrac1221​, over n=h+tn=h+tn=h+t flips:

h+1n+2=(1−ε) hn+ε⋅12,ε=2n+2.\frac{h+1}{n+2}=(1-\varepsilon)\,\frac hn+\varepsilon\cdot\frac12,\qquad\varepsilon=\frac2{n+2}.n+2h+1​=(1−ε)nh​+ε⋅21​,ε=n+22​.

Check: 1−ε=nn+21-\varepsilon=\tfrac n{n+2}1−ε=n+2n​, so (1−ε)hn=hn+2(1-\varepsilon)\tfrac hn=\tfrac h{n+2}(1−ε)nh​=n+2h​, and ε⋅12=1n+2\varepsilon\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac1{n+2}ε⋅21​=n+21​; together h+1n+2\tfrac{h+1}{n+2}n+2h+1​.

Coin B (n=2n=2n=2, ε=12\varepsilon=\tfrac12ε=21​): 12⋅0+12⋅12=14=0+12+2\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14=\tfrac{0+1}{2+2}21​⋅0+21​⋅21​=41​=2+20+1​.

Coin A (n=4n=4n=4, ε=13\varepsilon=\tfrac13ε=31​): 23⋅34+13⋅12=12+16=23=3+14+2\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac34+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12+\tfrac16=\tfrac23=\tfrac{3+1}{4+2}32​⋅43​+31​⋅21​=21​+61​=32​=4+23+1​.

More flips shrink ε\varepsilonε, so the data soon outweigh the two imagined flips.

Laplace moves the count ε=2n+2\varepsilon=\tfrac2{n+2}ε=n+22​ of the way to 12\tfrac1221​; more flips, smaller pull.

1 · Learning by counting · D · Today

Label smoothing gives every class an imagined count

An image classifier with K=3K=3K=3 classes (cat, dog, fox) learns from labelled photos. Recall Laplace: (1−ε) hn+ε⋅12(1-\varepsilon)\,\tfrac hn+\varepsilon\cdot\tfrac12(1−ε)nh​+ε⋅21​.

targetk=(1−ε) [k=cat]+ε/K\text{target}_k=(1-\varepsilon)\,[k=\text{cat}]+\varepsilon/Ktargetk​=(1−ε)[k=cat]+ε/K, where [k=cat][k=\text{cat}][k=cat] is 1 for cat, else 0.

ε=0.15, K=3\varepsilon=0.15,\ K=3ε=0.15, K=3: 1−ε=0.851-\varepsilon=0.851−ε=0.85, ε/K=0.05\varepsilon/K=0.05ε/K=0.05 (we take 0.15 so this is round). Cat 0.85⋅1+0.05=0.90.85\cdot1+0.05=\cM{0.9}0.85⋅1+0.05=0.9, dog and fox 0.85⋅0+0.05=0.050.85\cdot0+0.05=0.050.85⋅0+0.05=0.05; sum 0.9+0.05+0.05=10.9+0.05+0.05=10.9+0.05+0.05=1.

Label smoothing is Laplace's rule for classes: no class gets target 0.

1 · Learning by counting · D · Today

With the hard target, the over-sure prediction wins

Cross-entropy loss: −∑ktargetkln⁡pk-\sum_k\text{target}_k\ln p_k−∑k​targetk​lnpk​, where pkp_kpk​ is the model's probability for class kkk. Lower is better.

For a cat photo the hard target is (1,0,0)(1,0,0)(1,0,0): only the cat term survives, so the loss is −ln⁡pcat-\ln p_\text{cat}−lnpcat​.

prediction (cat, dog, fox)pcatp_\text{cat}pcat​loss −ln⁡pcat-\ln p_\text{cat}−lnpcat​
(0.9, 0.05, 0.05)(0.9,\,0.05,\,0.05)(0.9,0.05,0.05)0.90.90.90.1050.1050.105
(0.98, 0.01, 0.01)(0.98,\,0.01,\,0.01)(0.98,0.01,0.01), over-sure0.980.980.980.020\cO{0.020}0.020

The over-sure prediction gets the lower loss, so training pushes pcatp_\text{cat}pcat​ toward 1, as counting pushed θB\theta_BθB​ to 0 after two tails.

Under the hard target, more certainty always means a lower loss.

Next: the friend stops telling us the coin

Counting needs to know which coin made each flip. Now the friend reports only "HH".

A language model is trained on question → answer pairs. The reasoning written in between, the trace zzz, is never in the data.

2 · Hidden variables · Connection

Next: count with soft labels

The posterior says HH is 0.9 coin A. How many heads should HH give to coin A?
Answer. 1.8 = 0.9 × 2 heads. Computing the 0.9 is the E-step (expectation); counting fractional heads and dividing is the M-step (maximization) of expectation–maximization (EM).

Soft-label every record, count fractions, divide: expectation–maximization.

3 · Expectation–maximization · A · Idea

EM: guess the coins, soft-label the records, count, repeat

Goal: the θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​ with the largest log-likelihood ℓ=ln⁡p(HH)+ln⁡p(HT)+ln⁡p(TT)\ell=\ln p(\text{HH})+\ln p(\text{HT})+\ln p(\text{TT})ℓ=lnp(HH)+lnp(HT)+lnp(TT), where p(HH)p(\text{HH})p(HH) is the model's chance of record HH.

A circle: with θ\thetaθ we could label the records; with labels we could count θ\thetaθ. Break the circle with a guess.

E-step (expectation): Bayes' rule turns the guess into soft labels, each record's chance of coin A.

M-step (maximization): count heads ÷ flips for each coin, a record counting only by its share.

Why a guess is fine: no round ever lowers ℓ\ellℓ, so each round's guess fits at least as well as the last.

Each round needs only the flips and the last guess, never the true coin.

M-step: maximize each path's log, weighted by its soft label. Coins: θA=2.3/3\theta_A=2.3/3θA​=2.3/3.

Why "expectation": the M-step maximizes ∑nEz∼qt(n)[ln⁡pθ(x(n),z)]\sum_n\mathbb E_{z\sim q_t^{(n)}}\big[\ln p_\theta(x^{(n)},z)\big]∑n​Ez∼qt(n)​​[lnpθ​(x(n),z)], the expected complete-data log-likelihood (record and coin together). It is not ℓ\ellℓ itself but an easy stand-in: every term is the log of one path, with no log of a sum, so it splits into counts. Raising it raises ℓ\ellℓ; Section 4 proves this.

E: infer the hidden part. M: fit as if it were seen, with weights.

A guarantee, not luck: EM climbs.

4 · Why EM climbs · C · What it does not promise

Climbing is not reaching the top: the flat start never moves

Start with identical coins, θA=θB=12\theta_A=\theta_B=\tfrac12θA​=θB​=21​. E-step: HH's two paths are both 12⋅12⋅12=18\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac1821​⋅21​⋅21​=81​, so the chance of A is 1/81/8+1/8=12\tfrac{1/8}{1/8+1/8}=\tfrac121/8+1/81/8​=21​; the same for HT and TT.

Each record has p=18+18=14p=\tfrac18+\tfrac18=\tfrac14p=81​+81​=41​, so ℓ=3ln⁡14=−4.159\ell=3\ln\tfrac14=-4.159ℓ=3ln41​=−4.159. Recall: from (34,14)(\tfrac34,\tfrac14)(43​,41​) EM reaches ℓ=−3.989\ell=-3.989ℓ=−3.989 at θA=0.789\theta_A=0.789θA​=0.789 (or 0.211, the coins renamed).

4 · Why EM climbs · D · Today

A variational autoencoder learns the E-step's guess

For an image xxx, the hidden code zzz is many real numbers, so the posterior cannot be computed exactly. A variational autoencoder (VAE) (Kingma & Welling, International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2014) trains an encoder with weights φ\varphiφ to output the guess qφ(z∣x)q_\varphi(z\mid x)qφ​(z∣x).

4 · Why EM climbs · Connection

Next: replace the coins by bell curves

Nothing in the proofs of Lemma 1 and Theorem 4 used coins: only an observed xxx, a hidden zzz, and a model pθ(x,z)p_\theta(x,z)pθ​(x,z).

The points 0, 1, 4, 5 come from two bell curves. In EM, what plays the hidden coin?
Answer. The bell: hidden, picked first, then the point is drawn from it. This is a Gaussian mixture.

Same E-step, same M-step, same climb: now EM clusters points.

5 · Mixture models · A · Idea: k-means

k-means: join the nearest centre, then move to the average

k-means (Lloyd, 1982), the most widely used clustering method, repeats two steps until nothing changes. Run it on 0, 1, 4, 5 from a poor guess: centres 0 and 1 (in class, step through it with the button). Score J=J=J= sum of (point − its centre)2^22; smaller is tighter.

Assigneach point joins the nearest centre: a hard label, 1 or 0, never 0.989.
Moveeach centre goes to the plain average of the points that joined it.

Two rounds from the poor start (0, 1): centres 0.5 and 4.5, the middles of {0, 1} and {4, 5}.

5 · Mixture models · C · Theorem

Theorem 5: k-means is EM with bells of width zero

Theorem 5 (k-means as a limit). Take a Gaussian mixture with equal weights πk\pi_kπk​ and one shared width σ\sigmaσ, held fixed (not re-estimated), and let σ→0\sigma\to0σ→0. Then EM's E-step becomes "assign each point to its nearest centre" and its M-step becomes "move each centre to the plain average of its points": EM becomes k-means.
a share is a soft vote; shrinking every bell turns it into a hard vote for the nearest centre.

On the line: at the midpoint 2.5 both distances are 1.5, so both heights are equal and the share is 12\tfrac1221​ for every σ\sigmaσ; as σ→0\sigma\to0σ→0 the curve becomes a step there, exactly k-means' border between centres 1 and 4.

Soft labels harden into hard ones; weighted averages become plain averages.

5 · Mixture models · Appreciate

k-means or EM? Hard labels are fast; soft labels keep the doubt

k-meansOne nearest-centre test per point: fast. Assumes round groups of equal size.
EMKeeps the doubt (point 2: 0.82). Can also learn each group's weight (πk\pi_kπk​ = average share) and width.
Shared riskBoth only improve their score (EM: log-likelihood up; k-means: JJJ down), so a poor start can stop at a poor answer. Fix: several starts, or k-means++ (Arthur & Vassilvitskii, 2007).
PracticeRun k-means first, then EM from its centres; scikit-learn's GaussianMixture does this by default.

One family: EM is k-means that admits doubt; k-means is EM that refuses it.

5 · Mixture models · D · Today

Vector search: find the stored texts nearest to a question

Setting: a chatbot answers from a library of texts. Each text is stored as a vector, a list of numbers in which similar meanings lie close together; an embedding model is a network that turns a text into its vector. Retrieval-augmented generation: find the texts nearest the question, then answer with them.

coin gamemixturevector search record HH↔point xxx↔one text's vector coin A or B↔group↔cell of similar texts θA\theta_AθA​↔centre μk\mu_kμk​↔cell centre which coin?↔nearest centre↔file a text in its cell
Cost: the slow way compares the question with every stored vector: 1,000,000 distances per question for a million texts, and many questions per second.

Finding the nearest vectors is the bottleneck; k-means' nearest-centre step cuts it.

5 · Mixture models · D · Today, step by step

k-means cells: 64 distance computations instead of 240

Built once: the 240 points of the four-group animation are the stored vectors; k-means gives 4 centres, and each vector is filed in its nearest centre's cell, 60 per cell.

Step 1: distances from the query (1.5, 1.2) to the 4 centres (blue 3.54, orange 0.81, green 4.62, purple 2.97). Orange centre (2.06, 1.78): 0.562+0.582=0.65=0.81\sqrt{0.56^2+0.58^2}=\sqrt{0.65}=0.810.562+0.582​=0.65​=0.81, the nearest.

Step 2: compare with that cell's 60 vectors only; the nearest (ringed) lies at distance 0.13. Total 4+60=4+60=4+60= 64, not 240.

At scale: 1,000,000 vectors in 1,000 cells of about 1,000: 1,000+1,000=2,0001{,}000+1{,}000=2{,}0001,000+1,000=2,000 distances; 1,000,000÷2,000=5001{,}000{,}000\div2{,}000=5001,000,000÷2,000=500 times fewer (Jégou et al., 2011). Price: a neighbour just across a cell border can be missed.

k-means' nearest-centre step, reused as an index: search a cell, not the library.

5 · Mixture models · D · Today

A mixture of experts: mixture weights that depend on the input

Setting: a language model reads text one token (a word or a piece of one) at a time. A layer holds several smaller networks, the experts. A small router scores each expert, and a softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to 1 (here 0.62, 0.21, 0.12, 0.05, illustrative).

mixture: p(x)=∑kπk N(x∣μk,σ2)p(x)=\sum_k\pi_k\,\mathcal N(x\mid\mu_k,\sigma^2)p(x)=∑k​πk​N(x∣μk​,σ2)
experts: p(y∣x)=∑kπk(x) pk(y∣x)p(y\mid x)=\sum_k\cM{\pi_k(x)}\,p_k(y\mid x)p(y∣x)=∑k​πk​(x)pk​(y∣x)

Here xxx = the text read so far (the input); the predicted next token yyy plays the role of the mixture's point.

coin gamemixturemixture of experts coin A or B↔group kkk↔expert kkk chance ½↔weight πk\pi_kπk​↔router weight πk(x)\pi_k(x)πk​(x) p(HH∣A)p(\text{HH}\mid A)p(HH∣A)↔bell N(x∣μk,σ2)\mathcal N(x\mid\mu_k,\sigma^2)N(x∣μk​,σ2)↔prediction pk(y∣x)p_k(y\mid x)pk​(y∣x) record HH↔point xxx↔next token yyy

Why bother: the model holds many experts' parameters, yet each token pays only for the few experts it runs.

Same sum as a mixture (Jacobs et al., 1991); only the weights now depend on the token.

5 · Mixture models · D · Today, step by step

Top-2 routing on one token: run two experts, skip two

Step 1: the text is "The capital of France is". For the token "is", the router gives the 4 experts weights 0.62, 0.21, 0.12, 0.05 (illustrative; they sum to 1).

Step 2: keep the two largest, 0.62+0.21=0.830.62+0.21=0.830.62+0.21=0.83, and rescale to sum to 1: 0.620.83=0.75\tfrac{0.62}{0.83}=0.750.830.62​=0.75, 0.210.83=0.25\tfrac{0.21}{0.83}=0.250.830.21​=0.25.

Step 3: run only experts 1 and 2. Their chances that the next token is "Paris" (illustrative) are 0.9 and 0.5, so the layer outputs 0.75⋅0.9+0.25⋅0.5=0.800.75\cdot0.9+0.25\cdot0.5=\cG{0.80}0.75⋅0.9+0.25⋅0.5=0.80.

At scale: Mixtral (Jiang et al., 2024) has 8 experts per layer and runs 2 per token: 28\tfrac2882​, a quarter of the expert computation. There each expert outputs a vector, and the layer mixes those vectors with the same kind of weights (here 0.75, 0.25).

Top-2 hardens the router's weights, as σ → 0 hardened EM's shares into k-means.

5 · Mixture models · Connection

Next: the coin may switch between flips

So far one hidden group per record. Now the friend may switch coins between flips: one hidden coin per flip, kept with chance ¾, switched with ¼.

Three flips, each with its own hidden coin. How many coin sequences are there?
Answer. 8 =2⋅2⋅2=2\cdot2\cdot2=2⋅2⋅2. For 100 flips, 21002^{100}2100: too many to list.

Hidden chains: the sum over sequences, done step by step.

6 · Hidden chains · A · Idea

If the coin can switch between flips, the coins form a hidden chain

Goal: the posterior of each flip's coin, and p(flips)p(\text{flips})p(flips), without listing every sequence.

In the two-coin game one hidden coin made both flips of a record. Now the friend may switch coins between flips, so every flip has its own hidden coin.

A hidden Markov model: each coin depends only on the coin before (Lecture 2's chain), and each flip only on its own coin. Early speech recognizers were built on it.

A hidden chain links the coins flip to flip; on H, H, T we will find flip 2's coin and p(H, H, T)p(\text{H, H, T})p(H, H, T).

One coin sequence: multiply one number per arrow

Rules of the switching game: the first coin is A or B with chance ½; between flips the friend keeps the coin with chance ¾, switches with ¼; A shows H with ¾, B with ¼.

AAA: multiply its six arrows: 12⋅34⋅34⋅34⋅34⋅14=342⋅45=812048\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac{3^4}{2\cdot4^5}=\cG{\tfrac{81}{2048}}21​⋅43​⋅43​⋅43​⋅43​⋅41​=2⋅4534​=204881​.

Weight =3k/2048=3^k/2048=3k/2048, where kkk = number of 34\tfrac3443​-arrows (2048=2⋅45)(2048=2\cdot4^5)(2048=2⋅45): AAA k=4k=4k=4 → 81, ABA k=1k=1k=1 → 3.

6 · Hidden chains · B · On the coins: the shortcut

Cut every sequence at flip 2: the part before × the part after

Recall the sequences with coin A at flip 2: AAA 81, AAB 81, BAA 9, BAB 9 (× 2048), 180 in all.

Why it factors: the part after flip 2 depends only on the coin at flip 2 (each coin depends only on the coin before), so both ways in share the same two ways on.

Group them (distributive law): (27128+3128)⏟all ways in×(316+316)⏟all ways on=30128⋅616=1802048\underbrace{\big(\tfrac{27}{128}+\tfrac{3}{128}\big)}_{\text{all ways in}}\times\underbrace{\big(\tfrac{3}{16}+\tfrac{3}{16}\big)}_{\text{all ways on}}=\tfrac{30}{128}\cdot\tfrac{6}{16}=\tfrac{180}{2048}all ways in(12827​+1283​)​​×all ways on(163​+163​)​​=12830​⋅166​=2048180​ ✓

Why a pair label: each cell is the chance of (coin at flip 1, coin at flip 2); the diagonal (green) means the coin was kept. Both tables have coin A at flip 1 with 0.8 and at flip 2 with 0.75, yet keep 0.95 or 0.65. Single soft labels cannot fix the keep chance.

This EM for hidden chains is Baum–Welch (Baum et al., 1970), older than the name "EM".

6 · Hidden chains · D · Today

Tokenizers learn where to cut words by EM over hidden cuts

A language model reads text in pieces (tokens). No one labels where to cut "noon"; the Unigram tokenizer learns it by EM. Pieces (1–2 letters only): n, o, no, on, oo, each 1/5 at first.

coin chaintokenizer hidden coin sequence↔hidden cut, e.g. no|on flips H, H, T↔letters n, o, o, n heads chance↔piece probability keep / switch chance↔none: pieces drawn independently soft label γt\gamma_tγt​↔posterior of a cut, given the letters forward message αt\alpha_tαt​↔αk\alpha_kαk​ = chance of all cuts of the first kkk letters

e.g. α2\alpha_2α2​ = chance(n|o) + chance(no) =125+15=625=\tfrac1{25}+\tfrac15=\tfrac{6}{25}=251​+51​=256​.

A cut's chance = product of its pieces: 4 pieces 1/625, 3 pieces 5/625, 2 pieces 25/625; all 5 cuts: (1+5+5+5+25)/625 = 41/625. Speech recognition (CTC) runs the same sums over audio–letter alignments.

T. Kudo, “Subword regularization,” Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL) 2018; used in SentencePiece.

Cuts are hidden like coins; forward–backward adds over all cuts without listing them.

6 · Hidden chains · Connection

Next: when even the shortcut is too big

Forward–backward works because each coin touches only its neighbours. A hidden chain of thought (100 words a language model writes before its answer, each from a 50,000-word vocabulary) has 50,000100≈1047050{,}000^{100}\approx10^{470}50,000100≈10470 possible values, and each word depends on all earlier ones: no small messages.

How can we still get a soft label, such as HH's p(A∣HH)=0.9p(A\mid\text{HH})=0.9p(A∣HH)=0.9, without adding up every way?
Answer. Replay and count: Monte Carlo, as in Lecture 4.

Replace the exact E-step by samples.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · A · Idea

The E-step's sum can be impossible, yet running the model forward is cheap

Goal: run EM when the hidden variable has far too many values to add up.

Recall: the E-step needs the posterior pθ(z∣x)=pθ(x,z) /∑z′pθ(x,z′)p_\theta(z\mid x)=p_\theta(x,z)\,/\sum_{z'}p_\theta(x,z')pθ​(z∣x)=pθ​(x,z)/∑z′​pθ​(x,z′) of the hidden zzz given a record xxx such as HH, at the guess θA=34,θB=14\theta_A=\tfrac34,\theta_B=\tfrac14θA​=43​,θB​=41​. The sum has one term per value of zzz.

Adding up every zzz can be hopeless; running forward and keeping the matches is cheap. Monte Carlo EM uses such draws.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · A · Idea

Replay the game and keep the runs that match the record: the kept runs follow the posterior

To draw the coin for HH without computing p(HH)p(\text{HH})p(HH): replay the game at the guess θA=34,θB=14\theta_A=\tfrac34,\theta_B=\tfrac14θA​=43​,θB​=41​ (fair toss for a coin, flip it twice) and keep a run only if it shows HH. Shown: 32 replays at their expected counts; a fair toss sends 32⋅12=1632\cdot\tfrac12=1632⋅21​=16 runs to each coin.

No sum was computed: we only ran the game forward and compared. This is rejection sampling. Its cost: 32−10=2232-10=2232−10=22 of the 32 runs are thrown away. The keep rate 10/3210/3210/32 is exactly p(HH)p(\text{HH})p(HH), the sum we never computed, so rare records waste most runs.

Kept runs show A : B = 9 : 1, so each kept run's coin is a posterior draw: A with chance 0.9.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · C · Definition

Monte Carlo EM: draw m hidden values per record, then fit as if they were told

Definition (Monte Carlo EM; G. C. G. Wei and M. A. Tanner, J. Amer. Statist. Assoc., 1990). Records x(1),…,x(N)x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(N)}x(1),…,x(N); start from θ0\theta_0θ0​; choose mmm, the number of draws per record. For t=0,1,2,…t=0,1,2,\dotst=0,1,2,…:
E-step: for each record nnn, draw mmm hidden values (for example by replay-and-keep):
z(n,1),…,z(n,m) ∼ pθt(z∣x(n))z^{(n,1)},\dots,z^{(n,m)}\ \sim\ p_{\theta_t}\big(z\mid x^{(n)}\big)z(n,1),…,z(n,m) ∼ pθt​​(z∣x(n))
z(n,j)z^{(n,j)}z(n,j) = the jjj-th draw for record nnn.
M-step: maximum likelihood with each draw as a told label of weight 1m\tfrac1mm1​:
θt+1=arg⁡max⁡θ ∑n=1N1m∑j=1mln⁡pθ(x(n),z(n,j))\theta_{t+1}=\arg\max_\theta\ \sum_{n=1}^N\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\ln p_\theta\big(x^{(n)},z^{(n,j)}\big)θt+1​=argθmax​ n=1∑N​m1​j=1∑m​lnpθ​(x(n),z(n,j))

Each draw weighs 1/m1/m1/m; as m→∞m\to\inftym→∞ the fractions become the posteriors: EM again.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · D · Today

Teaching a language model to reason from answers is the replay-and-keep game

coin gamereasoning model hidden coin zzz↔hidden reasoning trace zzz record HH↔correct final answer θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​ (what EM learns)↔the model's weights toss chance π\piπ (½ in our game)↔how often the model writes each kind of reasoning posterior of the coin given HH↔posterior of the reasoning given the question and the correct answer replay, keep HH↔sample, keep correct count and divide↔fine-tune on kept texts

The training data hold only questions and final answers; the reasoning is hidden, like the coin.

Self-Taught Reasoner, STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) and Reinforced Self-Training with EM, ReST-EM (Singh et al., 2023) run this loop; ReST-EM names its two steps E and M.

Sample, keep the correct, fine-tune: Monte Carlo EM with a reasoning as the coin.

8 · Trusting the fit · C · Theorem

More unknowns than free numbers means no unique fit

Theorem 8 (counting test). If a model has more unknowns than one record's distribution has free numbers, the parameters are not identifiable: near a typical setting, a whole curve of settings gives the same distribution.
more unknowns than free numbers: some change of the unknowns is invisible in the data. Passing (unknowns ≤ free numbers) does not prove uniqueness.
(π,θA,θB)↦(p(0), p(2))(\pi,\theta_A,\theta_B)\mapsto\bigl(p(0),\,p(2)\bigr)(π,θA​,θB​)↦(p(0),p(2))
3 unknowns, 2 free numbers.
SSS, the slope table (the Jacobian): slope of each free number along each unknown, 2×32\times32×3
3 columns in a 2-D plane are linearly dependent: some step v≠0v\ne0v=0 has Sv=0Sv=0Sv=0.
steps along vvv change neither p(0)p(0)p(0) nor p(2)p(2)p(2)
True at every nearby setting, so following vvv traces a curve of equal fits (constant-rank theorem). ■\blacksquare■

Count before you fit: 3 unknowns but 2 free numbers guarantees a ridge.

8 · Trusting the fit · D · Today

A learned code is a hidden coin, and its axes can be turned freely

A variational autoencoder (VAE) gives each image xxx a hidden code z=(z1,z2)z=(z_1,z_2)z=(z1​,z2​); a decoder turns zzz into an image. We hope z1z_1z1​ means pose and z2z_2z2​ colour.

prior: the standard normal p(z)=12πe−(z12+z22)/2p(z)=\tfrac1{2\pi}e^{-(z_1^2+z_2^2)/2}p(z)=2π1​e−(z12​+z22​)/2, which depends only on the distance from 0: round
coin gameVAE coin A or B↔code z∈R2z\in\mathbb R^2z∈R2 record HH↔image xxx θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​↔decoder weights swap A ↔ B↔flip or permute the code axes ridge of equal fits↔circle of equal fits, one per angle

Why: rotate every code by an angle and let the decoder rotate back first. The round prior gives the rotated code the same density, so every image keeps its likelihood. So training lands on one angle by chance.

Like the ridge, rotations give endlessly many equally good codes.

8 Trusting the fitRestart from several guesses; keep the best log-likelihood ℓ\ellℓ.
Theorem 8 (counting test): more unknowns than free numbers ⇒ no unique fit (a ridge).		 Unknowns π=p(A), θA, θB\pi=p(A),\ \theta_A,\ \theta_Bπ=p(A), θA​, θB​: 3.
Two flips: p(h)p(h)p(h) = chance of hhh heads.
p(0)+p(1)+p(2)=1p(0)+p(1)+p(2)=1p(0)+p(1)+p(2)=1: 2 free numbers <3<3<3, a ridge.
Three flips: p(0)+⋯+p(3)=1p(0)+\dots+p(3)=1p(0)+⋯+p(3)=1: 3 free =3=3=3, pinned.

More draws buy precision slowly; more observed flips decide whether the answer is unique.

Research questions

Open questions: today's coin game, far larger

Wasted draws
To draw the coin given HH, keep only reruns showing HH: chance 12⋅34⋅34+12⋅14⋅14=1032\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac{10}{32}21​⋅43​⋅43​+21​⋅41​⋅41​=3210​. Rerun ↔ reasoning trace; HH ↔ correct answer. Can we sample correct traces without the waste? (Phan et al., 2023)
Trap or peak
At (12,12)(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(21​,21​) each record has chance 14\tfrac1441​, so ℓ=3ln⁡14=−4.159\ell=3\ln\tfrac14=-4.159ℓ=3ln41​=−4.159; every soft label is 12\tfrac1221​, so EM never moves. When does a spectral estimate (one pass over data averages) start EM near the peak? (Zhang et al., 2016)
Meaningful codes
Two flips: 3 head counts whose chances sum to 1, so 2 free numbers. Three flips: 4 counts, 3 free. Extra flip ↔ extra observed label (e.g. time). Which extra observations pin down a network's hidden code? (Hyvärinen & Morioka, 2016)

Today's coin game, scaled up: wasted draws, good starts, pinning down the hidden code.
